topicTitle: What is AI? History and Evolution of AI
prompt: Explain the Turing Test. What are its limitations?
modelAnswer:
Proposed by Alan Turing (1950) in 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence'. A human interrogator interacts in text with a machine and a human without seeing them. If the interrogator cannot reliably tell which is the machine, the machine is said to have passed.

Capabilities required to pass:
• Natural Language Processing
• Knowledge Representation
• Automated Reasoning
• Machine Learning

Limitations:
• Tests only imitation of behaviour, not real understanding (Searle's Chinese Room argument).
• Not reproducible or mathematically analysable.
• Machine may deliberately make human-like mistakes to pass.

topicTitle: What is AI? History and Evolution of AI
prompt: Describe the history and evolution of Artificial Intelligence from 1943 to the present.
modelAnswer:
[Period | Key Events]
• 1943-1955 Gestation | McCulloch & Pitts artificial neuron (1943); Hebbian learning (1949); Turing Test (1950); first neural network computer SNARC (1951)
• 1956 Birth | Dartmouth Workshop - John McCarthy coins 'AI'; Logic Theorist by Newell & Simon
• 1956-1974 Early enthusiasm | General Problem Solver, LISP (1958), ELIZA chatbot (1966), Shakey the robot
• 1974-1980 First AI Winter | Over-promising, Lighthill report, limited computing power, funding cut
• 1980-1987 Expert systems boom | XCON, MYCIN; Japan's Fifth Generation project; backpropagation revived
• 1987-1993 Second AI Winter | Collapse of LISP machine market, expert systems too costly to maintain
• 1990s Intelligent agents | Probabilistic methods, Deep Blue beats Kasparov (1997)
• 2000s Big data | Machine learning, Watson wins Jeopardy! (2011)
• 2012 onwards Deep learning | AlexNet (2012), AlphaGo (2016), Transformers (2017), generative AI and LLMs (2020s)

Reasons for the revival after each winter:
• Availability of large datasets (Big Data).
• Powerful hardware - GPUs/TPUs.
• Better algorithms - deep neural networks, reinforcement learning.
• Commercial success in speech, vision and recommendation.
Conclusion: AI has moved from symbolic, rule-based systems to data-driven learning systems that now work in everyday products.

Rationality:
Rationality depends on four things: (1) the performance measure, (2) the agent's prior knowledge of the environment, (3) the actions it can perform, (4) its percept sequence to date. Conclusion: A clear PEAS specification is the first step in agent design because it fixes what 'good behaviour' means and what the agent can sense and do.

topicTitle: Types of Agents: Simple Reflex, Model-based, Goal-based, Utility-based, Learning Agents
prompt: Explain Simple Reflex Agent and Model-based Reflex Agent with block diagrams.
modelAnswer:
Simple Reflex Agent:
Selects action on the basis of the current percept only, ignoring history. Uses condition-action rules (if-then).
function SIMPLE-REFLEX-AGENT(percept):
    state  <- INTERPRET-INPUT(percept)
    rule   <- RULE-MATCH(state, rules)
    return rule.ACTION
• Works only if environment is fully observable.
• Fast and simple but cannot handle unseen situations; can loop infinitely.
• Eg: Thermostat, automatic door, vacuum agent with if dirty then suck.

Model-based Reflex Agent:
Maintains internal state describing the unobserved parts of the world, using (1) how the world evolves and (2) how its own actions affect the world - the transition model and sensor model.
• Handles partial observability.
• state ← UPDATE-STATE(state, last action, percept, model); then rule matching.
• Eg: Self-driving car tracking vehicles out of view.

topicTitle: Types of Agents: Simple Reflex, Model-based, Goal-based, Utility-based, Learning Agents
prompt: Explain the five types of agents with neat block diagrams, working and examples.
modelAnswer:
1. Simple Reflex Agent:
Acts on the current percept via condition-action rules. No memory. Suitable only for fully observable environments. Eg: thermostat.
Sensors -> [What the world is like now] -> [Condition-action rules] -> Actuators

2. Model-based Reflex Agent:
Keeps an internal state updated using a model of 'how the world evolves' and 'what my actions do'. Handles partial observability. Eg: self-driving car.
Sensors -> [State + World model] -> [Condition-action rules] -> Actuators

3. Goal-based Agent:
Along with the model, it has a goal that describes desirable situations. Uses search/planning to find action sequences achieving the goal. More flexible - changing the goal changes the behaviour. Eg: GPS navigation.
Sensors -> [State + Model] -> [What happens if I do action A?] -> [Goals] -> Actuators

4. Utility-based Agent:
Uses a utility function to map a state to a real number representing the degree of happiness. Chooses the action with maximum expected utility. Handles conflicting goals and uncertainty. Eg: taxi choosing the safest + fastest route.

5. Learning Agent:
Can improve with experience and operate in initially unknown environments. Four components:
• Performance element - selects external actions.
• Critic - gives feedback on how well the agent is doing against a fixed performance standard.
• Learning element - makes improvements using the critic's feedback.
• Problem generator - suggests exploratory actions leading to new experiences.
[Agent | Memory | Goal | Utility | Learns]
• Simple reflex | No | No | No | No
• Model-based | Yes | No | No | No
• Goal-based | Yes | Yes | No | No
• Utility-based | Yes | Yes | Yes | No
• Learning | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes

Problem formulation:
Process of deciding what states and actions to consider given a goal. Steps: goal formulation → problem formulation → search → execution. Abstraction removes irrelevant detail so the state space is manageable.

State space:
The set of all states reachable from the initial state by any sequence of actions. Represented as a graph (nodes = states, edges = actions) or tree (search tree).

Missionaries & Cannibals formulation:
• State: (M, C, B) = missionaries and cannibals on the left bank, B = boat side (L/R).
• Initial: (3, 3, L). Goal: (0, 0, R).
• Actions: move 1M, 1C, 2M, 2C or 1M+1C across.
• Constraint: on neither bank may cannibals outnumber missionaries (unless there are no missionaries).

(3,3,L) -> (3,1,R) -> (3,2,L) -> (3,0,R) -> (3,1,L) -> (1,1,R)
-> (2,2,L) -> (0,2,R) -> (0,3,L) -> (0,1,R) -> (0,2,L) -> (0,0,R)

prompt: Explain Breadth First Search with algorithm and properties.
modelAnswer:
BFS expands the shallowest unexpanded node first, using a FIFO queue.
BFS(problem):
    frontier <- queue with initial node ; explored <- {}
    loop:
        if frontier empty: return FAILURE
        node <- frontier.POP()          # FIFO
        if GOAL-TEST(node): return SOLUTION(node)
        explored.add(node)
        for each child of node not in frontier/explored:
            frontier.INSERT(child)
[Property | Value]
• Complete | Yes (if b is finite)
• Optimal | Yes, if all step costs are equal
• Time | O(b^d)
• Space | O(b^d) - major drawback

topicTitle: Informed (Heuristic) Search: Greedy Best-First Search, A* Algorithm
prompt: Write the A* algorithm and state its properties.
modelAnswer:
A*(start, goal):
    OPEN <- {start}; CLOSED <- {}
    g(start)=0; f(start)=h(start)
    while OPEN not empty:
        n <- node in OPEN with lowest f = g + h
        if n == goal: return path
        move n to CLOSED
        for each successor m of n:
            cost = g(n) + c(n,m)
            if m new or cost < g(m):
                g(m)=cost; f(m)=g(m)+h(m); parent(m)=n; add m to OPEN
• Complete (finite branching, cost ≥ e > 0).
• Optimal if h is admissible (tree) / consistent (graph).
• Optimally efficient - no other algorithm using the same h expands fewer nodes.
• Weakness: space O(b^d) - stores all nodes.

topicTitle: Heuristic Function Design and Admissibility / Consistency
prompt: How are heuristic functions designed? Explain relaxed problems, dominance and effective branching factor with examples.
modelAnswer:
Methods to design heuristics:
• Relaxed problem: remove constraints from the original. Cost of exact solution to relaxed problem is an admissible heuristic. 8-puzzle: if tile can move to any adjacent square → Manhattan; to any square → misplaced tiles.
• Pattern databases: store exact costs for sub-problems (e.g. fixed subset of tiles).
• Learning from experience: learn h(n) from solved examples using features.
• Combining heuristics: h(n) = max(h1(n), h2(n), ... ) stays admissible.

Dominance:
If h2(n) ≥ h1(n) for all n, h2 dominates h1 and is more informed. Always choose the dominating heuristic provided it is cheap to compute.

Effective branching factor (b*):
If A* generates N nodes and the solution depth is d, then b* is the branching factor of a uniform tree with depth d containing N+1 nodes: N + 1 = 1 + b* + (b*)² + ... + (b*)^d. A good heuristic has b* close to 1. Conclusion: Well designed, admissible and consistent heuristics keep A* optimal while reducing the search effort drastically.

Allows occasionally 'bad' moves to escape local maxima. A temperature T starts high (many bad moves accepted) and is gradually lowered according to a cooling schedule.

• Applications: VLSI layout, travelling salesman, scheduling.

topicTitle: Adversarial Search: Minimax Algorithm, Alpha-Beta Pruning
prompt: Explain the Alpha-Beta pruning algorithm with a suitable game-tree example showing which branches are pruned.
modelAnswer:
ALPHA-BETA(s, alpha, beta):
    if TERMINAL(s): return UTILITY(s)
    if MAX's turn:
        v = -inf
        for each child c:
            v = max(v, ALPHA-BETA(c, alpha, beta))
            alpha = max(alpha, v)
            if alpha >= beta: break      # beta cut-off
        return v
    else: (MIN's turn)
        v = +inf
        for each child c:
            v = min(v, ALPHA-BETA(c, alpha, beta))
            beta = min(beta, v)
            if alpha >= beta: break      # alpha cut-off
        return v

Example:
Root (MAX) with children B, C (MIN). B leaves: 3, 5 ; C leaves: 2, 9.
Start: alpha=-inf, beta=+inf
B: leaf 3 -> v=3 ; leaf 5 -> v stays 3 (MIN) -> B=3 ; root alpha=3
C: leaf 2 -> v=2 ; beta=2 <= alpha=3 -> PRUNE leaf 9
Root value = max(3, 2) = 3  (same as minimax)
• Effectiveness depends on move ordering: best-first ordering gives O(b^(m/2)); random ordering ¬O(b^(3m/4)).
• Pruning never changes the root value, only reduces work.
• Improvements: killer-move heuristic, transposition tables, iterative deepening, evaluation functions at cut-off depth.

prompt: Explain propositional logic: syntax, semantics, logical equivalences, inference rules and limitations. Prove using a truth table that P → Q is equivalent to ¬P ∨ Q.

Syntax and semantics:
Propositional logic deals with atomic statements that are either true or false, combined using connectives ~, ^, v, →, ↔. Semantics are given by truth tables.

Important equivalences:
• De Morgan: ¬(P ∧ Q) = ¬P ∨ ¬Q ; ¬(P ∨ Q) = ¬P ∧ ¬Q
• Contrapositive: P → Q = ¬Q → ¬P
• Implication: P → Q = ¬P ∨ Q
• Double negation: ~¬P = P
• Distributivity: P ∧ (Q ∨ R) = (P ∧ Q) ∨ (P ∧ R)

Inference rules:
[Rule | Form]
• Modus Ponens | P, P → Q therefore Q
• Modus Tollens | ¬Q, P → Q therefore ¬P
• And-elimination | P ∧ Q therefore P
• Hypothetical syllogism | P → Q, Q → R therefore P → R
• Resolution | P ∨ Q, ¬P ∨ R therefore Q ∨ R

Proof: P → Q = ¬P ∨ Q:
[P | Q | P → Q | ¬P ∨ Q]
• T | T | T | T
• T | F | F | F
• F | T | T | T
• F | F | T | T
Both columns are identical, hence equivalent.

Limitations:
• Cannot express relations over objects (no variables/quantifiers).
• Very large number of propositions needed (e.g. 'all humans are mortal' must be written per person).
• No way to represent general rules compactly → need first-order logic.

topicTitle: First-Order Predicate Logic: Syntax, Quantifiers (Concept)
prompt: Explain the syntax and semantics of first-order predicate logic with quantifiers. Convert English statements into FOL and discuss the rules for quantifiers.
modelAnswer:
Syntax elements:
[Element | Description | Example]
• Constants | Name specific objects | Ram, 5, India
• Variables | Range over objects | x, y
• Predicates | Properties/relations | Student(x), Loves(x,y)
• Functions | Map objects to objects | FatherOf(x)
• Connectives | ~, ^, v, →, ↔ | 
• Quantifiers | ∀x (for all), ∃x (there exists) | ∀x Human(x) → Mortal(x)
• Equality | = | FatherOf(Ram) = Dasharath

Quantifier rules:
• Typical pairing: Universal (A) with implication (→); Existential (E) with conjunction (^).
• Duality: ¬∀x P = ∃x ¬P ; ¬∃x P = ∀x ¬P.
• Order matters: ∀x ∃y Loves(x,y) (everyone loves someone) differs from ∃y ∀x Loves(x,y) (someone is loved by everyone).

Translations:
All birds fly              : Ax Bird(x) -> Flies(x)
Some cats are black        : Ex Cat(x) ^ Black(x)
Everyone loves someone     : Ax Ey Loves(x,y)
No dog is a cat            : Ax Dog(x) -> ~Cat(x)

Semantics:
An interpretation maps constants to objects, predicates to relations and functions to mappings over a domain. A sentence is true in a model if it holds under that interpretation.

topicTitle: Inference in First-Order Logic: Forward Chaining, Backward Chaining, Resolution (Concept)
prompt: Explain forward chaining and backward chaining with an example. Prove 'West is a criminal' from the given KB.
modelAnswer:
KB (definite clauses): (1) American(x) ∧ Weapon(y) ∧ Sells(x,y,z) ∧ Hostile(z) → Criminal(x); (2) Owns(Nono, M1); Missile(M1); (3) Missile(x) ∧ Owns(Nono,x) → Sells(West,x,Nono); (4) Missile(x) → Weapon(x); (5) Enemy(x,America) → Hostile(x); (6) American(West); Enemy(Nono,America).

Forward chaining:
Facts: Owns(Nono,M1), Missile(M1), American(West), Enemy(Nono,America)
Pass 1: Sells(West,M1,Nono) [rule 3], Weapon(M1) [rule 4], Hostile(Nono) [rule 5]
Pass 2: Criminal(West) [rule 1]  -> goal reached

Backward chaining:
Goal Criminal(West)
  <- American(West) .......... fact OK
  <- Weapon(y) <- Missile(y) .. y = M1 OK
  <- Sells(West,M1,z) <- Missile(M1), Owns(Nono,M1)  z = Nono OK
  <- Hostile(Nono) <- Enemy(Nono,America) OK
=> Criminal(West) PROVED

FOL resolution (concept):
• Convert to CNF: eliminate →, move ~ inward, standardise variables, Skolemise (remove E), drop A, distribute v over ^.
• Resolve clauses using unification; refutation of negated goal gives empty clause.
• Complete for FOL (semi-decidable).

topicTitle: Rule-Based (Production) Systems
prompt: Describe production systems in detail: components, control strategies (forward/backward), conflict resolution and an example. Mention their characteristics.
modelAnswer:
Components:
• Global database / working memory: current facts.
• Production rules: IF (condition) THEN (action).
• Control system / inference engine: chooses and applies rules.

Control strategies:
• Forward chaining (data-driven).
• Backward chaining (goal-driven).
• Conflict resolution: rule ordering, specificity (most specific rule first), recency, refraction (do not refire).

Example (car diagnosis):
R1: IF engine_does_not_start AND lights_dim THEN battery_weak
R2: IF battery_weak THEN recharge_or_replace_battery
Facts: engine_does_not_start, lights_dim
Forward: R1 fires -> battery_weak ; R2 fires -> recommend recharge

Types of production systems:
• Monotonic / non-monotonic
• Commutative (order of rule application irrelevant) / partially commutative
• Decomposable
Conclusion: Production systems are simple and powerful for encoding heuristic expert knowledge and form the basis of expert systems.

topicTitle: Bayes' Theorem and its Application to AI Reasoning
prompt: Explain Bayes' theorem and its application to AI reasoning (diagnosis, spam filtering, Naive Bayes classifier). Solve a numerical problem.
modelAnswer:
Bayes' theorem allows an agent to update beliefs when new evidence arrives and to reason from effects to causes (diagnostic reasoning): P(cause | effect) = P(effect | cause) P(cause) / P(effect).

Applications:
• Medical diagnosis: P(disease | symptoms).
• Spam filtering: P(spam | words).
• Naive Bayes classifier: assume features independent given the class: P(C | x1..xn) proportional to P(C) x product P(xi | C); choose class with max value.
• Fault diagnosis, speech recognition, robotics localisation.

Numerical:
Three machines M1, M2, M3 produce 50%, 30%, 20% of items with defect rates 1%, 2%, 3%. An item is found defective; find P(it came from M1).
P(D) = 0.5x0.01 + 0.3x0.02 + 0.2x0.03 = 0.005 + 0.006 + 0.006 = 0.017
P(M1|D) = (0.01 x 0.5) / 0.017 = 0.005 / 0.017 = 0.294  (~29.4%)

Advantages and limitations:
• Principled and incremental updating; handles uncertainty.
• Needs prior and likelihood values; full joint tables grow exponentially → motivates Bayesian networks.
• Naive independence assumption rarely exactly true but works well in practice.

topicTitle: Certainty Factors and Rule-Based Uncertainty (Overview)
prompt: What is a certainty factor? How are CFs combined?
modelAnswer:
A certainty factor CF(h, e) in [-1, +1] expresses the net belief in hypothesis h given evidence e: CF = MB - MD (measure of belief minus measure of disbelief).
• Rule: IF e THEN h (CF = c). CF(h) = c x CF(e).
• AND: CF(e1 AND e2) = min(CF1, CF2). OR: max(CF1, CF2).
• Two rules supporting the same hypothesis (both positive): CF = CF1 + CF2 (1 - CF1).
Example: CF1 = 0.6, CF2 = 0.5
CF = 0.6 + 0.5 x (1 - 0.6) = 0.6 + 0.2 = 0.8

R2: CF = 0.5 x 0.6 = 0.30

• Data needed | Expert estimates | Priors, likelihoods

unitTitle: Unit 5.0: Introduction to Machine Learning & AI Applications
topicTitle: Overview of Regression and Classification: Linear Regression, k-NN, Decision Trees
prompt: Explain the decision tree algorithm (ID3) with entropy and information gain. Construct a decision tree for a small dataset.
modelAnswer:
Decision tree: tree of attribute tests; leaves hold class labels. ID3 picks the attribute with highest information gain at each node.
Entropy(S)  = - sum p_i log2 p_i
Gain(S, A)  = Entropy(S) - sum (|Sv|/|S|) x Entropy(Sv)

Example (Play Tennis style, 14 samples: 9 Yes, 5 No):
Entropy(S) = -(9/14)log2(9/14) - (5/14)log2(5/14) = 0.940
Outlook: Sunny(2Y,3N)=0.971, Overcast(4Y,0N)=0, Rain(3Y,2N)=0.971
Gain(Outlook) = 0.940 - (5/14)(0.971) - (4/14)(0) - (5/14)(0.971) = 0.247  <- highest
=> Root = Outlook; Overcast -> Yes; split Sunny on Humidity, Rain on Wind

Advantages / disadvantages:
• Easy to understand, handles categorical and numeric data, no scaling needed.
• Prone to overfitting → use pruning; unstable to small data changes → use ensembles (Random Forest).
Variants: C4.5 (gain ratio), CART (Gini index).

unitTitle: Unit 5.0: Introduction to Machine Learning & AI Applications
topicTitle: Introduction to Artificial Neural Networks: Perceptron, Basic Architecture (Concept)
prompt: Explain the architecture of an artificial neural network (biological analogy, MLP) and the backpropagation learning process.
modelAnswer:
Biological analogy:
Dendrites → inputs; synapses → weights; cell body → summation + activation; axon → output.
  Input layer      Hidden layer(s)       Output layer
   (x1) o ------>  o  o  o  ------>    o (y1)
   (x2) o ------>  o  o  o  ------>    o (y2)
   (x3) o ------>  o  o  o
   fully connected, feed-forward

Training with backpropagation:
1. Initialise weights randomly.
2. Forward pass: compute outputs layer by layer.
3. Compute loss (e.g. MSE / cross-entropy).
4. Backward pass: compute gradients with the chain rule.
5. Update weights: w ← w - η x dLoss/dw (gradient descent).
6. Repeat over epochs until loss converges.

Notes:
• Learning rate, epochs, batch size are hyper-parameters.
• Deep networks (many hidden layers) learn hierarchical features → deep learning; CNNs for images, RNNs/Transformers for sequences.
• Issues: overfitting (use dropout, regularisation), vanishing gradients (use ReLU).

Ethical issues:
• Bias and discrimination, privacy and surveillance, lack of transparency (black box).
• Accountability for autonomous decisions (e.g. accidents of self-driving car).
• Misuse: deepfakes, misinformation, autonomous weapons, cyber-attacks.
• Copyright and intellectual property issues with generative AI.

Societal impact:
• Positive: productivity, healthcare access, education, accessibility, scientific discovery.
• Negative: job displacement, inequality (digital divide), over-dependence, energy consumption of large models.

AI for SDGs:
[SDG | AI contribution]
• SDG 2 Zero hunger | Precision agriculture, crop disease detection
• SDG 3 Good health | Disease diagnosis, drug discovery, telemedicine
• SDG 4 Quality education | Personalised learning, language tools
• SDG 7 Clean energy | Smart grids, demand forecasting
• SDG 11 Sustainable cities | Traffic management, waste management
• SDG 13 Climate action | Climate modelling, emission monitoring
Way forward: regulations (e.g. EU AI Act, India's AI governance guidelines), ethics committees, audits, open standards and AI literacy.
